newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korea mulls slicing soybean imports, Japan calm.
newsitem.headline: Korea mulls slicing soybean imports, Japan calm.

text.p: South Korean buyers are mulling cutting imports of soybean and soy products while Japanese importers reacted calmly to the strong overnight rally of Chicago soybean futures prices, traders said on Wednesday.

Soybean prices on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) jumped after the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) revised its March 1 quarter stocks figure for soybeans to 1.056 billion bushels, 22 million bushels below the figure released on Monday.
"We are planning to cut our soybean imports by more than 10 percent in the coming third quarter due to current strong prices," a senior manager of South Korea's Shindongbang Corp said.
Traders said the company imported 35,000 tonnes to 50,000 tonnes of U.S. soybeans a month.

Dealers said Korean companies which have to buy tens of thousands of tonnes of soymeal for arrival in May were caught in a tight fix by surging meal prices on the CBOT, where the May contract closed near the US$10 a ton upper limit at $293.00.

The May CBOT soybean contract closed on Tuesday up 19-3/4 at $8.75-1/2 a bushel. The spot May 1997 contract in the CBOT's Project A after-hours trading system was quoted at $8.71-3/4 a bushel at 0735 GMT on Wednesday.

A trader with South Korea's National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF) said suppliers were offering U.S. soymeal at around $350 a tonne C&F, compared with $340 a tonne C&F for the same product a day before.
The NLCF trader said nearby soybean futures prices are likely to touch $9.50-$10.00 a bushel in the coming weeks, while soymeal prices are seen touching $310-$330 a ton.
Other South Korean feed milling companies will probably trim their soymeal imports and will have to find alternative sources, the traders said.
"We have no choice but to find other alternatives...to avoid a production cost hike," a trader with Cheiljedang Corp said.

In Japan, dealers said there would have been a sharper reaction to the USDA revision of its stocks figure if it had happened in June or July. Japanese buyers had also put on coverage up to May shipments, they added.
"We expected buying from local end-users if the USDA announced bullish figures. But local users are calmer than expected," a soybean trader in Japan said.
Taiwane buyers ignored the rise in soybean prices. They were more worried that the foot-and-mouth disease which has crippled the hog industry on the island.
Edible oil makers are cutting imports due to a soymeal inventory build-up caused by the pork industry crisis.

"The massive pig slaughter has significantly reduced feed demand for soymeal, forcing processors to cut volume," Hui Shung Agriculture and Food Co buyer Jack Lee told Reuters. "People seem to have under-estimated the impact of the hog crisis on the soybean industry," he added.
Taiwan imported about 2.4 million tonnes of soybeans in 1996 and traders have said the hog disease could reduce the island's 1997 imports by at least 10 percent.
Buyers in Japan and Korea also shrugged off news of a strike in the Brazilian port of Santos due to begin on Wednesday and reports that heavy rains may disrupt loadings at the port of Paranagua.
"At this stage, we are not worring so much about the Brazilian news. But we will closely watch further developments," the Cheiljedang trader said.
"We're carefully monitoring developments there. But there's no serious concern here at the moment," an official of a major soybean crusher in Japan said.
